clauses.reason: The clause ended by its own terms on 1950-08-05. The order forbids any change, except by agreement, in the conditions out of which the Boston & Albany Railroad Company dispute arose, from the order's date and for thirty days after the board made its report to the President. The board's report is shown by the dated letter of transmittal, July 6, 1950 (later event, a reviewed factual event; submission date, receipt by the President may have been later). The letter misprints the order number as 10138; the report's own first page, parties and the June 6, 1950 date identify Executive Order 10130. Thirty days after July 6, 1950 is August 5, 1950; the end is recorded inclusive of August 5, and the exclusive reading (ending when August 5 begins) is the alternative. The board's own commands (to investigate and to report) were performed when the report was submitted on July 6, 1950, which is not later than the standstill's end. The thirty-day report deadline is not an end. Executive Order 12553, signed February 25, 1986, revokes this order by number and is recorded as the later formal disposition; it is not the first end because the order's own term had already ended. No saving provision appears in it.

research_rationale:
Identity. The held Federal Register text (15 FR 3539, issue of June 8, 1950, PDF page 1) is headed Executive Order 10130. It creates an emergency board under section 10 of the Railway Labor Act to investigate the dispute between the Boston & Albany Railroad Company (New York Central Railroad Company, lessee) and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, and the dossier records its signing date as June 6, 1950. The Civil Service Commission notices printed on the same page are separate documents and are not part of the order. Inventory. The order is one block of text with four commands: create a three-member board, bar members from any interest in an employee organization or carrier, require the board to report within thirty days of the order, and forbid any change except by agreement in the conditions out of which the dispute arose from the order's date until thirty days after the board has made its report. I read the whole text; the verified one-clause inventory covers all of it and no operative sentence lies outside it. End. The last command to end is the no-change command, which by its own terms runs until thirty days after the board made its report. The report date comes from the dated letter of transmittal of Presidential Emergency Board report No. 86, held as PDF bytes (jobs/astra-source-retention/output/pdf/3b006fcbfcf2701f2e28105441441e08b7ab9955843399808d9620892e1079ba.pdf, SHA-256 verified) and cited here as a reviewed factual event. The letter is dated Boston, Mass., July 6, 1950 and says the board tenders its report herewith; I read the page image, which shows July 6, 1950 (the text layer misreads the year). The cover and the closing line of the report also carry July 6, 1950. Report identity. The letter identifies the creating order as Executive Order 10138 dated June 6, 1950. Executive Order 10138 is a different order, signed July 3, 1950, about the Toledo dock companies. The report's own first page states that the board was created by Executive Order No. 10130 dated June 6, 1950 and reproduces the order's operative paragraphs, and the parties, carrier and union named in the letter, on the cover and in the body (Boston & Albany Railroad Company, Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, NMB Case A-3392) match this order. I treat the number in the letter as a misprint; the order number, parties and June 6, 1950 date all point to this order. Thirty days after July 6, 1950 is August 5, 1950 (25 days remain in July after the 6th, and 5 more fall in August). I record the end as August 5, 1950, inclusive of that day, under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21; the exclusive reading, under which the command ends when August 5 begins, is the alternative. The letter date is the date of submission; receipt by the President may have been later, and no held source gives a receipt date. The held eight-page report shows no supplemental report, reconvening or extension. Later events. Executive Order 12553 (signed February 25, 1986, 51 FR 7237, Federal Register of March 3, 1986) lists this order by number in a table of orders revoked together with any amendments to them; it came 36 years after the own-terms end and is recorded as the formal disposition. No amendment of this order is held. Searches. The U.S. Code search (release point through 2026-10-09), the eCFR search as of 2026-10-14 and the Office of the Federal Register disposition-note search returned no other instrument affecting this order. Savings: none found.

savings.reason: Executive Order 12553, read in full, is one revoking sentence, a table of revoked orders, an editorial note and the date line, with no saving or transition provision. The commands of this order were a one-time board investigation and report and a standstill that expired by its own terms on 1950-08-05; no held source shows any appointment, transfer or right created under it that survived.
